title: Stories of success from the Arctic to Papua New Guinea

sections.heading: Body
sections.text:
Posted on April, 22 2026
The Blue Corridors for Turtles initiative aims to close critical gaps in marine turtle and ocean conservation. © Tom Vierus / WWF-US
The deepening crises of climate change and nature loss threaten the future of life on Earth. WWF is taking action, focusing our efforts where we can achieve the greatest positive impact. From tackling shipping fuel emissions in the Arctic to supporting community-led conservation in Papua New Guinea, here's some good news on the progress we are making.
Governments agree on greater migratory species protection
WWF has worked long and hard to safeguard species that cross national borders, with habitat loss, wildlife overexploitation and infrastructure barriers all accelerating their decline.
So we warmly welcome news from the latest UN meeting on migratory species where governments agreed on new or enhanced protection for 40 species – including the striped hyena, thresher sharks and the snowy owl.
There was a strong new resolution on the capture of untargeted species (bycatch) by fishers, a major threat to marine wildlife around the world. And there were also strengthened commitments to ensuring the free movement of species across land and waters, including a new resolution that supports the WWF-led initiative to provide “blue corridors” for safer marine turtle migration.
We are seeking to identify areas that are critical for marine turtle populations – a vital first step toward enabling conservation measures that reverse their decline.
Global retail business sets nature impact targets
Businesses have a big role to play in helping to deliver on global UN targets for putting nature on the path to recovery by 2030. So it’s great to see H&M Group becoming the first company in its sector, and the third to date, to set science-based targets – validated by the Science Based Targets Network (SBTN) – to reduce its impact on land-based nature.
WWF worked closely with H&M Group, a long-term partner of ours since 2011, to help assess risks in their supply chain and support the development of credible targets, such as avoiding deforestation and supporting local projects that benefit people and nature.
Our technical experts contributed to the development of the SBTN target guidelines, which are grounded in what science tells us the planet needs to thrive.
Unlocking high-impact investments in Africa
A new WWF-backed facility aims to help African enterprises scale up impactful climate-adaptation and biodiversity-positive solutions that benefit people and nature.
The WWF Nectar Fund, supported by the Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation (Norad) and Norfund, will provide grants and tailored technical assistance. By strengthening companies’ business models, impact measurement and investment readiness, the fund aims to accelerate capital flows into landscapes that are home to communities and ecosystems on the front lines of climate change and nature loss.
We believe that the initiative will prove attractive to investors, who will benefit from a more secure pipeline of opportunities backed by WWF’s technical expertise and on-the-ground presence in key African landscapes.
It’s also the latest milestone in WWF’s Bankable Nature Solutions journey – a finance approach that has structured investments worth billions in companies delivering water stewardship, sustainable land use and measurable impact on nature and climate.
Reducing shipping fuel emissions in Arctic waters
The heavy fuel oil used by ships is the world’s most polluting and hazardous fuel – contributing to emissions of black carbon, the second largest contributor to global warming after CO2.
WWF has long been pushing for the introduction of Emission Control Areas (ECAs) in Arctic and North Atlantic waters to help curb air pollution caused by shipping fuel emissions. So we are delighted that new Canadian Arctic and Norwegian Sea ECAs have now entered into force.
The regulations will reduce harmful fuel emissions by requiring all ships to use low-sulphur fuel or exhaust gas cleaning systems (scrubbers) – and new ships to face new emission limits for nitrogen oxides.
Our work continues to close down potential loopholes in the new regulations and for the adoption of an ECA in the North Atlantic.
Safeguarding forests and communities in Viet Nam
Tung oil is connecting forest communities to global markets. © WWF-Viet Nam
A WWF-backed partnership in Viet Nam has created Quang Tri province’s first formal tung seed export channel to India, improving incomes for ethnic minority households and reducing pressure on forests.
Extracted from the seeds of the tung tree, tung oil is in growing global demand as a non-toxic, renewable alternative to petroleum-based products and for many other industrial uses.
Paco and Van Kieu ethnic minority communities have long collected and sold the seeds in Quang Tri province, but, until now, have depended entirely on middlemen – leading to price fluctuations, unreliable demand and low incomes. A more reliable market would strengthen the case for forest protection, as well as provide increased economic security for seed collectors, 90% of whom are women.
So WWF has helped address this by brokering a connection between the communities, the Sepon Group and local authorities. Sepon Group committed to purchasing tung seeds above market price, giving collectors a stable and improved return.
Sepon Group processes the seeds into oil for more added value before export – and is also utilizing the seed’s pericarp to make pallets for energy and organic fertilisers.
Mexico sees rise in monarch butterfly numbers
Every year, eastern monarch butterflies travel up to 2,800 miles from Canada and the US to overwintering sites in the forests of Mexico’s Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve – a challenging journey made even harder due to habitat loss and climate change.
Two new reports from WWF-Mexico and partners show that, despite these challenges, conservation efforts are having a positive impact on their population. During the 2025-2026 over wintering season in Mexico, scientists found an increase in monarch numbers – reflected by a 64% increase in the area occupied by migratory monarchs.
WWF-Mexico is working with partners to promote sustainable forest management, forest restoration and ecological tourism for the benefit of both butterflies and local communities. Conservation efforts are also taking place in the US, with WWF-US urging habitat restoration and reductions in neonicotinoid pesticides, one of the leading drivers of monarch decline.
Permanent sturgeon fishing ban in Bulgaria
Sturgeons are among the most endangered species globally due to the loss of habitats, disruption of migration routes, poaching and the illegal trade in caviar. So we welcome news that the Bulgarian government has introduced a permanent ban on sturgeon fishing in the Danube River and the Black Sea after issuing repeated short-term bans since 2011.
WWF has long worked for the protection of these critically endangered species and the broader restoration of biodiversity in the region. Over the years, we have carried out long-term population research, implemented restocking programmes by releasing nearly 100,000 juveniles into the Danube, worked to identify and protect spawning habitats, and supported the introduction of stricter protection measures.
The scientific data and expertise of WWF-Bulgaria have been essential in justifying the need for a permanent ban and in guiding efforts to restore these species.
Solar initiative powers Congo Basin work
Forest elephants at Dzanga Bai, Dzanga-Sangha Protected Areas, Central African Republic. Photo Credit: ©Andy Issacson / WWF-US
In the Dzanga-Sangha protected areas of the Central African Republic – home to critical populations of elephants, gorillas, bongos and other wildlife – WWF is striving to build a sustainable future for people and nature.
The solar panels we installed and refurbished over the past five years are now powering nearly all electricity consumption within and surrounding the park.
Some of this directly supports our conservation work – enabling electrification of remote forest areas where park staff used to have no power, including an observation platform where critically endangered forest elephants can be studied. But communities are also big beneficiaries, with power provided to a nearby hospital, ecolodges for visitors, other local businesses and even a community football pitch.
This progress has been achieved by WWF's Energizing Communities and Conservation (ECCo) programme, which has delivered 24+ solar projects in Dzanga-Sangha and elsewhere in the Congo Basin.
You may also be interested to learn about our work with western lowland gorillas in Dzanga-Sangha – how efforts to habituate them to the presence of people has benefits for both gorillas and local communities.
Supporting locally led conservation in Papua New Guinea
WWF’s People Powering Biodiversity programme is currently working in five countries to help put local communities and Indigenous Peoples at the centre of conservation decision-making.
In Pomio district, a highly forested and biodiverse area of Papua New Guinea, the programme team is working with Indigenous communities to support the protection of their ancestral lands and waters from threats such as deforestation and infrastructure development.
We’ve been listening to the views of community members on mapping out proposed community conservation areas.
Elders shared their expertise with younger members of the community as they marked boundaries and identified sacred sites, rivers, hunting grounds and other places they believe should be protected for future generations. They also set out priorities for the species they want to conserve.
This vital first step will be followed by further WWF support on formalizing their proposed conservation areas, setting up governance groups and planning activities that safeguard their territories.
